articles.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO

top_comments: Some takes (and from talking to nvidia people):- Delaware precedent in Caremark has a very high bar for culpability of boards in matters like this. So I suspect the combination of DoJ saying they won't prosecute combined with this standard will successfully remove their individual liability.- I'm surprised this decision was completely unanimous at the board level, considering how they quickly forced him out. Full 180 in under two weeks.- The news media is really confusing selling chips to Megaspeed then hosting them in Malaysia (giving chinese companies access - afaik still legal under the old export regime) and Megaspeed smuggling these physical chips for hosting in Chinese data centers. Former was legal and second was not.- I would not be surprised if a pardon was mentioned at some point. Will be watching how state AGs end up getting involved. CA has already subpoenaed Nvidia for this.- There was a drum circle at Nvidia from employees who were petitioning to get him backDisclosure: I co-host a podcast that talks about this. More discussion if anyone is interested: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t8nLiELIhwA

Many people here are assuming Nvidia committed some kind of crime that would've been exposed if not for government intervention. Yes the US govt is corrupt but they're likely right that there's no actual evidence. If there was, it would've already leaked from whoever's been leaking all the intelligence so far.All of the stuff coming out has been pointing the other way. CIA/AG have both said they're unsure if the woman is a spy, US politicians briefed by intelligence have all said the same. Nvidia followed normal diligence in selling GPUs to a cloud provider in Southeast Asia (including visiting their data centers), then banned Megaspeed per government request in 2025. The idea that Nvidia knew they were smuggling hasn't been suggested by anyone involved in the actual investigations. Do people think Megaspeed told Jensen they were going to smuggle chips? What would be the possible benefit of this?The Congressional committees will be about Nvidia did enough extra diligence. And there's no criminal investigation of Nvidia, only against Megaspeed, contrary to what everyone's saying.The realistic risk for Nvidia isn't that executives get hauled off to jail for arguably weak diligence, it'd be more like Seagate's export control penalty (civil fine + audit requirements). But even then Seagate's case was way more clear cut.

“ In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”Feels like the most operative part of the statement.

This actually worked amazingly well.I tested a lot of sites.. a few that were already opened in my firefox, and a few many others.. Every single one of them rendered correctly.This is truly amazing.. a new browser written from scratch that actually works!The only minor issue: page scrolling is a bit jerky.. not much.. just a little bit.. it's noticeable.A huge lots of congratulations to the Ladybird team. What a wonderful accomplishment truly this is.

I really do hope that, down the road, Ladybird will take the fingerprinting problem seriously. What a modern browser truly needs IMO is a non-compliant JS mode that returns spoofed or randomized values across the entire userbase to effectively make identifying unique users far harder. Permissions should also be far more granular, and a website should not be allowed to know if the window or tab is active, and things like disabling selection or paste should not be allowed by default. In short, the browser should assume that all websites are hostile and present a very minimal and uniform surface by default.

I am seriously impressed, BRAVO for this! I have tried a few websites that I considered tricky (from overloaded news websites to some more esoteric like ProxMox) and all seems to be in order. I am seriously impressed by the latter, I honestly didn't expect NoVNC [web view for remote virtual display] to be even snappier than it is in Firefox.I don't know of course if this ever becomes my daily driver, but I am surely giving it a serious try starting now. I am super excited and supportive of the idea of a true alternative browser, that alone is my motivation.P.S. Scrolling feels strange. I think FF smooths the movement, whereas in Ladybird it follows my scrolling precisely and interprets my finger jitter too just :) And some fonts look a bit blurry. None of these will stop me from me trying it out.

articles.title: "Dario is hyping the dangers so OSS models are illegal and he stays in control"
articles.summary: "Dario is hyping the dangers so OSS models are illegal and he stays in control"

top_comments: > The widespread use of robust non-recovery encryption ultimately will devastate our ability to fight crime and terrorism.-- Louis Freeh, FBI director, in front of the senate, January 28th, 1998That was when he tried to outlaw open-source encryption. We're here all over again. What certainly does not change is how a lot of people are scared of users freedom.

Polarized group signaling makes everything into a false dichotomy. AI is not particularly dangerous _yet_. It probably will become increasingly dangerous though, especially if we don't take potential risks seriously.On the other hand, there is no urgent need to shut all of the research down. And AI is not against humans at all at this point. It's still a tool. I would argue the most powerful tool for potentially decreasing inequality and dramatically improving quality of life for the average person. But also could be used for oppression.So I say, let's have a culture of caution, but also focus on coming up with a system where the power of AI and robotics really benefits everyone and we avoid giving it more intelligence and autonomy than we can handle.

The most important thing to discuss in advocating for open-weight models is how to address their safety concerns. Highlighting e.g. the obvious conflicts of interest that Dario has is not enough to convince people to ignore the safety risks. We need a concrete counterproposal for how open-source models can proceed while mitigating these risks to acceptable levels.For example:1. Supposing that at some point in the future, open-source models can find and exploit software vulnerabilities, how do we e.g. protect critical infrastructure around the world?2. Supposing that at some point in the future, open-source models can walk a non-chemist through the process of making nerve gas, how do we prevent nerve agent attacks?3. Supposing that at some point in the future, open-source models can help a non-biologist design a novel pathogen, how do we prevent the resulting pandemic?These are not meant as rhetorical questions. They are real questions that need real answers. Personally I have no clue what the answer is, and would love to read some serious answers. I tried to order them from most to least imminent.

articles.title: Per Arm's request, this site will be discontinued on 4 December 2026 :(
articles.summary: Per Arm's request, this site will be discontinued on 4 December 2026 :(

top_comments: Hi, didn't expect to see this here, so adding a bit of info:They are requesting removal stating that I am using their trademarks and IP by hosting their documentation, which seems hard to work around while still keeping the site useful.People have contacted me offering to host mirrors, or suggesting I lawyer up or release the source code (sans Arm IP) to generate the same site for personal use. I'll be looking into all of these options.For those unfamiliar with this site until now: it's the ISA documentation, but with search and without all the popups and bloat. The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily.Thanks for the support, everyone! :)

This is why in most companies lawyers should report to an engineer (or someone who understands the business) who signs off on these things.Going after this merely makes life harder for people ultimately providing value/income to ARM.

Why would they threaten legal action over this? Surely documenting hardware should be fair use, right? Or are we somehow at the point where companies can decide who can even know how their publicly sold/release tech works?

articles.title: New York Bans Subscription and Post-Purchase Fees on Cars
articles.summary: New York Bans Subscription and Post-Purchase Fees on Cars

top_comments: This trend drives me nuts! I've bought a VW Multivan T7, second hand, amazing vehicle for my family. It comes with a set of options you can purchase, for example, extra LED colors for the interiors or Auto headlights, which I find it insane! So you are telling me this vehicle has the tech to auto regulate it's headlights but it sits behind me shelling out +€200 for it? This needs to be made illegal; Also, having lock in on where my data goes, effectively needing to pay VW to keep track of my vehicle position or battery status is just crazy; Europe needs to make mandatory all this data to be exposed internally to the user and let him decide what to do with it, either use VW services for convenience or ship it to some third party or self hosted open source service (along with choosing who provides Internet to your vehicle).

To answer parallel questions, this appears to not impact either SiriusXM or Tesla's enhanced cruise control.The senate bill[1] specifically exempts "navigation system updates, infotainment features, satellite radio, in-vehicle Wi-Fi, telematics services, roadside assistance, software-dependent driver assistance or driver automation features, or vehicle-connected services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation"This is pretty clearly aimed at the German automakers who were trying to put stuff like heated seats behind a subscription.1 - https://legislation.nysenate.gov/pdf/bills/2025/S9348A

Any car feature that doesn’t incur an ongoing cost to the manufacturer to maintain should be available post-purchase without any kind of subscription, this should be a federal law with back breaking financial penalties if they’re broken.
